nodes.label: Existing MARL evaluation suites do not treat generalization to novel situations as their primary objective.
Background-population per-capita return is measured as a secondary metric to detect harm to the wider population.
Each agent architecture was trained with 21 runs, one per substrate.
Exploiter agents and a random agent bound the performance range on each test scenario.
Solving Melting Pot's scenarios appears to require agents that model trust, reciprocity and deception.
Melting Pot is expected to get harder over time as improved agents are folded into its background populations.
No broadly accepted benchmark test set for MARL research existed.
The absence of a standardized MARL evaluation protocol has impeded progress in the field.
Melting Pot is an evaluation suite for multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Melting Pot uses reinforcement learning to create test scenarios instead of authoring them by hand.
Automated scenario generation is possible because one agent's behaviour forms part of another agent's environment.
Melting Pot contains more than 80 unique test scenarios.
Melting Pot revealed weaknesses in standard MARL algorithms that training performance alone did not show.
Focal-population per-capita return is Melting Pot's primary evaluation metric.
Measurement Layouts, a hierarchical Bayesian framework, is applied to infer capability profiles of multi-agent systems.
Inferred capability profiles predict future performance within the Melting Pot suite.
Higher prosocial capability does not reliably accompany higher contest score.
Top-performing submissions scored highest in scenarios where prosocial capability was not required.
Leading submissions appear to have exploited a weakness in the evaluation framework.
Some capabilities did not differentiate between submissions because the corresponding task demands were sparse.
Future competitions should use less sparse, non-duplicated task-demand meta-features.
Traditional internet trust mechanisms assume static, human-operated services and cannot meet the coordination needs of large-scale agent ecosystems.
State-of-the-art LLM agent frameworks exhibit prompt injection, sycophancy, nudge-susceptibility, hallucination, deception and misalignment.
The trust models underlying inter-agent protocols had not been systematically analysed.
The paper compares six trust models: Brief, Claim, Proof, Stake, Reputation and Constraint.
No single trust mechanism is sufficient on its own.
High-impact agent actions should be gated by Proof and Stake rather than by reputation or self-declared claims.
Trust should be tiered to stakes: light verification where impact is negligible, relentless verification where it is not.
Reputation mechanisms presume a persistent identity with behavioural continuity, sanction sensitivity and costly non-fungibility.
Language model agents are assemblages of mutable modules, any of which may change their behaviour.
Dissociativity leaves agents without grounding for identifiability, predictability, credibility and rehabilitability.
Reputation signals for dissociative agents become actively harmful rather than merely uninformative.
Identity-based, ex post, sanction-based governance is structurally inapplicable to language model agents.
Governance should target the operator and the protocol rather than the agent.
The binding constraint on AI is shifting from capability to coexistence.
The dominant AI research paradigm treats the world as an exogenous and stationary source of feedback.
Deploying an AI system induces endogenous non-stationarity, creating a train-test-deploy gap.
The more aggressively a system exploits historical regularities, the faster other actors make them obsolete.
A dynamic evaluation is one whose test distribution depends on the evaluated policy through adaptive counterparties.
No existing evaluation approach meets all the requirements for valid dynamic evaluation.
Institutions should be treated as design primitives rather than as context.
Artificial Organisational Intelligence is defined as an organisation's capacity to make its own knowledge legible and governable.
AOI is about organisations talking to themselves through regulated feedback loops, not about replacing them with AI.
Knowledge Organisation Infrastructure is a protocol for connecting disparate systems without homogenising them.
Ethnographic practice is transformed by this work, moving from observing hidden practices to building the loops that make them computable.
